summary:
Belgian law provides for legal gender recognition by self-determination. Under the Law of 25 June 2017, in force since 1 January 2018, a trans person changes registered gender and first names by declaration to the civil registrar, with no medical conditions, surgery or sterilisation attached. The Constitutional Court partially annulled that law on 19 June 2019; the Federal Justice Department states that applications continue to be handled under the existing procedure pending replacement provisions.

For minors the route is narrower. A person aged 12 to 16 may change a first name only. At 16 and 17, a change of sex marker requires parental consent together with a psychological opinion confirming that the decision is freely made.

The Brussels-Capital Region's own page on changing gender registration still lists a medical certificate attesting to sex change, and possibly a judicial or administrative decision, among the documents required alongside a valid identity document, and states that the procedure is free of charge and takes three to six weeks. That requirement conflicts with the federal self-determination regime and its current status is unresolved.

Discrimination, hate crimes and hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are prohibited. Prosecution is nonetheless hampered by the absence of a statutory definition: Belgian legislation does not define hate crimes and no code exists to record them as such, so violations of non-discrimination law that constitute criminal offences are prosecuted under general provisions.

Equality bodies Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men report rising violence and intimidation against LGBTQI people, with gay men and trans people especially affected. Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases Unia handled in a year, 35 per cent involved physical assault and 35 per cent serious intimidation.

A recurring pattern is the dating-app trap: perpetrators use fake profiles to arrange a meeting, then ambush the victim in an isolated place to rob, humiliate or assault them. In May 2025 the Brussels Criminal Court heard the case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims. Police have recorded a significant number of such incidents, and many go unreported because of fear or shame.

A 2019 study found that 90 per cent of LGBT people in Brussels had experienced verbal or psychological harassment.

Hate motive has been recognised in court. On 22 December 2014 a Liège jury convicted four people of the homophobic murder of Ihsane Jarfi, the first Belgian crime officially qualified as hate-motivated on grounds of sexual orientation.

Conversion practices were banned on 20 July 2023, with penalties of eight days to two years' imprisonment and fines of 208 to 2,400 euros.

A 2023 femicide law covers all gender-based homicide.

Marriage and adoption are open to same-sex couples on the same terms as opposite-sex couples, and lesbian couples have access to IVF. Since 1 January 2015 a mother's female partner is recognised as co-mother without an adoption procedure, removing an inequality that had persisted under the Civil Code.

Hostility at the level of major institutions is largely absent, but party politics has been a vector. The Flemish Block/Vlaams Belang and the National Front voted against same-sex marriage; Vlaams Belang later stated it would not campaign for repeal, and in 2019 its chairman condemned an MP who had criticised same-sex marriage and adoption. N-VA was criticised for joining a European parliamentary group containing homophobic parties.
tangentialFactors:
Medically unnecessary surgery on intersex infants remains legal in Belgium, although a Brussels court has held a hospital accountable for non-consensual interventions.

Sex between men was decriminalised in 1795 under the French penal code, but public-indecency laws and police harassment persisted for decades afterwards; article 372bis raised the age of consent to 18 for same-sex acts between 1965 and 1985, and was repealed on 18 June 1985 after a debate triggered by the case of the lesbian teacher Eliane Morissens.
localsOnly:
Requests to change a registered first name rose from 85 in 2012 to 187 in 2016, the year before the self-determination law was adopted.

A national survey of trans people in Belgium published in 2017 by the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men covers gender identity, coming out, openness, obstacles to living according to one's gender identity, being addressed according to experienced gender, official name and gender registration change, work, sex work, economic status and well-being.

Flemish Ministry of Health-funded LGBT organisations run lumi.be, a suicide-prevention project, and gendervonk.be, a suicide-prevention site aimed at trans youth.

Between 2006 and 2014, 70 LGBT domestic adoptions were recorded: 58 by male couples and 2 by female couples in Flanders, and 12 in the French Community.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific homicide count appears in the source inventory, so no comparison with Belgium's general homicide rate can be made and no severity estimate is offered here. The Unia figures are case counts handled by an equality body, not population rates.

The Brussels-Capital Region page listing a medical certificate as a requirement for changing gender registration has not been reconciled with the federal self-determination procedure; which document set a commune actually applies is unresolved.

The large survey of trans people in Belgium held by the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men dates from 2017, before the 2018 law took effect, and its findings are not itemised in the inventory.

The ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map entry gives an overall index score and per-category compliance without the underlying scores appearing in the inventory.
